scenes.tts: You have never met most of the viruses that will ever infect you. Yet your body already holds B cells whose receptors can bind them. How can a defense be ready for a molecule before it exists in your world? The answer is a rule called clonal selection.
scenes.visual: Row of lymphocytes each with its own receptor tip shape; a dashed unknown-virus box with a question mark; the question; then the rule name.
scenes.narration: You have never met most of the viruses that will ever infect you. Yet your body already holds B cells whose receptors can bind them. How can a defense be ready for a molecule before it exists in your world? The answer is a rule called clonal selection.

scenes.tts: In vertebrates, adaptive immunity is carried by lymphocytes, a kind of white blood cell. Each lymphocyte makes receptors of one specificity, and it makes them before it ever meets antigen. An antigen is the molecule a receptor binds. When antigen arrives, it binds only the few cells whose receptors already fit. Those cells divide into a clone, a population descended from that one cell.
scenes.visual: Antigen shape docks on the one cell whose tip fits; that cell turns green and divides into a row of identical cells.
scenes.narration: In vertebrates, adaptive immunity is carried by lymphocytes, a kind of white blood cell. scenes.tts: How does a body make millions of receptor shapes from a human genome of about twenty thousand protein-coding genes? The part of an antibody that binds antigen is not encoded as one piece. In each developing lymphocyte, the cell joins one V, one D, and one J segment for a heavy chain. This is called somatic recombination. At each joint, nucleotides are added or removed. That is junctional variation.

scenes.tts: Count the possibilities, using illustrative human numbers. Forty V times twenty-three D times six J gives five thousand five hundred twenty heavy chains. Light chains come in two kinds. Kappa gives two hundred combinations, and lambda gives one hundred twenty. That makes three hundred twenty light chains. Each B cell pairs one heavy chain with one light chain. Multiplying gives about one point eight million receptors, if every combination works. That is from fewer than one hundred fifty segments.
scenes.caption: Count the possibilities, using illustrative human numbers. 40 V x 23 D x 6 J gives 5,520 heavy chains. Light chains come in two kinds. Kappa gives 200 combinations, and lambda gives 120. That makes 320 light chains. Each B cell pairs one heavy chain with one light chain. Multiplying gives about 1.8 million receptors, if every combination works. That is from fewer than 150 segments.

scenes.tts: No antigen was needed to make any of these shapes. After a first response, which takes days to build, most of the expanded cells die. But memory B cells and memory T cells remain. A second encounter starts from a larger, already selected population. So the secondary response is faster and larger.
scenes.visual: Clone thins to a few memory cells; a sketch plot shows a slow small first response and a fast larger second.

scenes.tts: Some earlier theories held that antigen acts as a template, folding a general antibody into a matching shape. Clonal selection replaced that idea. Receptors are made first, by recombination. Antigen finds the cells that already fit, and they become a clone. Keep this rule. The antigen chooses. It does not shape.
scenes.visual: Crossed-out template idea beside the selection idea.
